findings.summary: The caption's first sentence is a series label rather than a hook, burying the actual attention-grabbing line in second position.
findings.evidence: "Part 2 of BASH CONTROL FLOW. `[[ 10 > 9 ]]` is false, and that one line has broken more deploy scripts than any missing semicolon."
findings.fix: Lead with the hook and demote the label: "`[[ 10 > 9 ]]` is false — and that one line has broken more deploy scripts than any missing semicolon. Part 2 of BASH CONTROL FLOW walks the whole branching surface of Bash…"

findings.summary: Page 1 teaches case's failure modes and branch terminators before ever showing case's syntax, so `*)`, `;;`, `;&` and `;;&` are used before they are defined.
findings.evidence: The page opens with "Ordering Kills" → callout "Put *) Last" ("`*)` is the catch-all default. Placed in the middle it swallows everything") and the "Branch Terminators" table, while the first actual `case` block — "case $1 in / -h|--help) usage ;; ... esac" — appears three blocks later under "Where case Shines".
findings.fix: Lead with the `case $1 in ... esac` example (plus the facts that patterns are globs, not regex, first match wins, and the word needs no quotes), then present the terminator table and the `*)`-ordering gotcha.

findings.summary: A code line in the counter-fix block is cut off at the block's right edge, truncating the redirection.
findings.evidence: Code reads `while read l; do ((c++)); done < <(gre` — the line stops mid-token at the block boundary instead of showing `<(grep ...)`.
findings.fix: Shorten the snippet (e.g. `done < <(grep x f)`) or reduce the code font size / allow wrapping so the full command fits inside the block width.

findings.summary: The final bullet block on page 3 explains three bugs whose subjects are not named until the table at the top of page 4, so the explanations arrive before the things they explain.
findings.evidence: Page 3 ends with: "If `b` fails, `c` runs too — a classic silent bug", "Braces expand before variables; use C-style `for`", "Always put a `sleep` inside a polling loop" — `b`, `c`, and braces have no antecedent on page 3. Page 4 then opens with "Two More Silent Ones" and the table rows ["`a && b || c`","not if/else"], ["`{1..$n}`","never expands"], ["tight poll loop","pins a core"].
findings.fix: Move those three bullets to page 4 directly under the table so each explanation sits beside the construct it names, and correct the heading "Two More Silent Ones" to match the three rows it introduces.

findings.summary: Boxes in the "Pick the Loop" flowchart overlap each other and are crossed by connector lines, hiding text.
findings.evidence: The `glob: for f in *` box sits on top of the `for x in "${arr[@]}"` box (a stray `g` is visible behind it), and a connector line runs straight through the `for (( i=0; i<n; i++ ))` box.
findings.fix: Re-layout the diagram with explicit non-overlapping node positions and route connectors around boxes, or increase the diagram's allotted height so nodes are not compressed into each other.

findings.summary: The wrap-up "choose the right construct" page is placed before two pages that still teach new material, so the handbook summarizes itself and then keeps going.
findings.evidence: Page 4 is "Choosing the Right Test & Loop" with "Pick the Test", "Pick the Loop", "Defensive Header" (`set -euo pipefail`), "Truthiness Recap" and "Quoting Rule of Thumb"; pages 5–6 then introduce unseen material — the status-code table (`127`, `126`, `130`, `137`), the retry-with-backoff pattern, and the entire lexicographic `<`/`>` topic — and page 5 even repeats a recap ("One-Line Recall") mid-stream.
findings.fix: Order the part as: case → read loop → gotchas → set -e/exit codes/verification → lexicographic `<` and `>` → the "Choosing the Right Test & Loop" summary last.

findings.summary: The description of `set -o pipefail` inverts which failing pipeline stage determines the exit status.
findings.evidence: "`pipefail` reports the FIRST failing pipe stage" — the Bash manual (Pipelines) states: "If pipefail is enabled, the pipeline's return status is the value of the last (rightmost) command to exit with a non-zero status, or zero if all commands exit successfully."
findings.fix: Change the bullet to "`pipefail` reports the LAST (rightmost) failing pipe stage".

findings.summary: A new numbered deep-dive on lexicographic comparison starts on page 5 under a page title about set -e and exit codes, splitting the 1–6 sequence across a page boundary.
findings.evidence: Page 5 has page_title "set -e, Exit Codes & Verification" but its last blocks are headings "1. What They Compare" and "2. No Escaping in [[ ]]"; page 6 is titled "Lexicographic < and >" with subtitle "Sorting Text, Not Math" and opens at "3. But [ ] Needs \<".
findings.fix: Move sections 1 and 2 onto page 6 so the whole numbered sequence lives under the "Lexicographic < and >" title, and keep page 5 to set -e, status codes, retry and verification.

findings.summary: `[ a < b ]` is claimed to create or truncate file `b`, but `<` is input redirection and never creates or truncates.
findings.evidence: "`[ a < b ]` silently creates or truncates the file `b`" — `<` opens `b` for reading; if `b` does not exist the command fails with "No such file or directory" and `[` never runs; truncation/creation is the behaviour of `>`.
findings.fix: Rewrite as: "`[ a < b ]` redirects stdin from the file `b` — it errors if `b` is missing and tests only `a`; the mirror-image `[ a > b ]` is the one that creates/truncates `b`."

findings.summary: The Q&A block is built on the false premise that an unescaped `<` inside `[ ]` truncates a file and creates an empty one.
findings.evidence: q: "Why did my test create an empty file?" / a_bullets: "You wrote `<` unescaped inside single `[ ]`", "Bash redirected stdin and truncated that name" — input redirection `<` cannot create or truncate; only `>` does.
findings.fix: Re-target the Q&A at `>`: "Why did my test create an empty file? You wrote `>` unescaped inside `[ ]` — Bash treated it as output redirection and truncated that name. Use `[[ ]]`, or escape it as `\>`." (A bare `<` instead produces a "No such file or directory" error.)

findings.summary: The caption's page count does not match the handbook it describes.
findings.evidence: caption: "Ten pages of dense field notes" — part 01 contains 7 pages and this part contains 6, i.e. 13 pages in total.
findings.fix: Update the shared caption to the real total ("Thirteen pages…") or drop the count.

findings.summary: The rename example applies the space substitution to the whole path, so it breaks whenever a parent directory contains a space.
findings.evidence: "find . -print0 | while IFS= read -rd '' f; do", "  mv -- \"$f\" \"${f// /_}\"" — for `./my dir/a b.txt` the target becomes `./my_dir/a_b.txt`, a directory that does not exist, and `mv` fails.
findings.fix: Substitute only the basename, e.g. `mv -- "$f" "${f%/*}/${##*/}"`-style: `d=${f%/*}; b=${f##*/}; mv -- "$f" "$d/${b// /_}"`, or restrict the example to `find . -maxdepth 1`.

findings.summary: The heading "Fields and Descriptors" promises descriptor content that does not appear until the unheaded bullets at the top of the next page.
findings.evidence: Page 1 heading "Fields and Descriptors" is followed only by the `IFS=: read -r user pass uid rest` and `find -print0` blocks; the descriptor material ("A nested read needs its own descriptor: `exec 3< other.txt`", "Then use `read -u 3` inside the outer loop") opens page 2.
findings.fix: Rename the page 1 heading to "Splitting Into Fields" and give the page 2 opening bullets their own heading such as "Extra Fields and Descriptors".

findings.summary: The cost model given for `while read` misstates its syscall behaviour.
findings.evidence: "`while read` is slow: roughly a syscall per line" — Bash's `read` probes the fd with `lseek`; on a non-seekable fd (a pipe) it falls back to unbuffered one-byte `read()` calls, i.e. a syscall per *character*, while on a seekable regular file it reads in ~128-byte buffered chunks, i.e. fewer syscalls than lines.
findings.fix: Replace with "`while read` is slow: from a pipe Bash reads one byte per syscall so it cannot over-consume input".

findings.summary: Page 3 re-poses the pipe-to-while subshell problem as an open question after page 2 has already diagnosed and fixed it.
findings.evidence: Page 2 diagram cards already state "cmd | while — loop runs in a subshell / variable writes vanish / counter ends up 0" and "done < <(cmd) — loop stays in this shell / variables survive"; page 3 then shows the same counter code and asks "Why does my counter print 0?" with answer "The `|` put the loop body in a subshell".
findings.fix: Keep the worked example and Q&A on page 3 and cut the page 2 cards to a one-line forward pointer, or drop the page 3 Q&A and keep only the code demonstration.

findings.summary: The flowchart's root label "which loop?" is duplicated, appearing both as a caption and inside the decision diamond.
findings.evidence: "which loop?" appears twice in the "Pick the Loop" panel — once in green italics above the chart and once inside the diamond node.
findings.fix: Remove the caption above the diagram and keep only the text inside the decision diamond.

findings.summary: `[[ B < a ]]` is annotated as ASCII order, which is false in the default en_US locale and contradicts the locale section on the next page.
findings.evidence: Page 5 code: "`[[ B < a ]]       # ASCII order`" vs page 6: "Under `en_US` the order folds case: a, A, b, B" and "`[[ B < a ]]    # false, aAbB`".
findings.fix: Annotate the page-5 line with its precondition, e.g. "`[[ B < a ]]   # true under LC_ALL=C; false under en_US`", or drop the ASCII claim and defer it to the locale section.

findings.summary: A code block demonstrating `[ ]`'s escaping requirement sits under the heading about `[[ ]]` needing no escaping, one page before the section that explains why.
findings.evidence: Under "2. No Escaping in [[ ]]" page 5 ends with the block "[ a \< b ]     # compares / [ a '<' b ]    # also compares / [ a < b ]      # opens file b!"; the explanation "`[` is a ==command==, so `<` is parsed as a **redirect**" only arrives on page 6 under "3. But [ ] Needs \<".
findings.fix: Move that code block to page 6 under "3. But [ ] Needs \<", leaving section 2 with only the `[[ $name > $max ]]` example.

findings.summary: Escaping the operator inside `[[ ]]` is described as a literal comparison, when it is actually a syntax error.
findings.evidence: "In `[[ ]]` the backslash is wrong — it makes Bash compare against the literal `\<`." — the Bash manual requires conditional operators to be unquoted to be recognised; `[[ a \< b ]]` yields "syntax error in conditional expression", not a comparison against a literal string.
findings.fix: Change to: "In `[[ ]]` the backslash is wrong — quoting the operator stops Bash recognising it, and the test dies with a syntax error in conditional expression."
